blind_spots.description: The entire design assumes x86-64 (AVX2/AVX-512, PCLMULQDQ) or ARM64 (NEON, PMULL). RISC-V with vector extensions (RVV), POWER (AltiVec), and WebAssembly SIMD have different capabilities and constraints. A truly portable solution needs an abstraction layer.
blind_spots.mitigation: Use portable SIMD libraries (e.g., std::simd in Rust nightly, or highway/simde) and test on WASM SIMD in addition to native targets.

blind_spots.description: Real-world CSV is messy: Excel uses different delimiters per locale (semicolons in Europe), some files use single-quote quoting, some use backslash escaping instead of quote doubling, some have BOM markers. Our SIMD approach hardcodes structural characters.
blind_spots.mitigation: Parameterize the SIMD classification LUTs so the delimiter, quote, and escape characters are configurable. Most of the architecture remains valid; only the classify stage needs runtime constants.

blind_spots.area: Very small files and high-latency startup
blind_spots.description: SIMD and two-phase architectures have setup overhead (profiling, buffer allocation, instruction cache warming). For files < 1MB, a simple scalar parser might be faster. We may be over-engineering for the small-file case.
blind_spots.mitigation: Implement a fast scalar fallback path that activates below a size threshold (e.g., < 64KB). Only engage the full SIMD pipeline for files above the break-even point.

blind_spots.description: mmap has issues: TLB pressure for very large files, inability to handle files from non-seekable sources (pipes, network streams, compressed archives), and platform-specific behavior on Windows vs. Unix.
blind_spots.mitigation: Support both mmap and streaming (read+buffer) modes. The structural indexing works with any contiguous buffer, not just mmap'd memory.

blind_spots.description: RFC 4180 allows newlines inside quoted fields. This means row boundaries cannot be determined independently of quote state — you need to know if you're inside a quote to know if a newline is a row terminator. This creates a serial dependency that limits how much we can parallelize Phase 1 across large input regions.
blind_spots.mitigation: Use CLMUL quote pairing to resolve this dependency in O(1) per 64-byte block. For parallel chunked processing of huge files, synchronize at chunk boundaries by scanning forward from each chunk start to find the first unambiguous row boundary (outside any quote).

blind_spots.description: For heavily numeric CSV files, Phase 2 (number parsing) may dominate Phase 1 (structural detection). Our design focuses on Phase 1 optimization but Phase 2 could become the bottleneck.
blind_spots.mitigation: Integrate SIMD-accelerated number parsing (Lemire's fast_float for floats, and SIMD integer parsing techniques). Consider batched number parsing where multiple fields are converted simultaneously.

blind_spots.description: Multi-threaded Phase 2 extraction requires synchronization for shared output buffers. Lock contention or false sharing could negate parallelism benefits.
blind_spots.mitigation: Use per-thread output buffers that are merged at batch boundaries. Ensure column buffers are cache-line-aligned to prevent false sharing.

blind_spots.description: We optimize parsing, but the consumer (pandas, R, Spark) may immediately copy our output into its own format, negating zero-copy benefits.
blind_spots.mitigation: Produce Arrow-compatible output directly. Arrow's C Data Interface enables zero-copy handoff to pandas (via PyArrow), R (via arrow R package), and Spark.

anomaly_results.constraint: What if the CSV has only 1 column?
anomaly_results.analysis: With 1 column, there are no comma delimiters. The structural detection simplifies to only newline scanning, which is essentially memchr on steroids. The CLMUL quote pairing still matters for quoted single-column values. The columnar materialization degenerates to a single-buffer write. Row prediction becomes trivial. Main optimization: maximize newline scanning throughput. This is actually the simplest case and should achieve near-memory-bandwidth throughput.
anomaly_results.insight: The architecture gracefully degenerates to specialized fast paths as column count decreases.

anomaly_results.constraint: What if every field is quoted and contains embedded commas and newlines?
anomaly_results.analysis: This is the adversarial case. Quote density is 100%, every comma and newline must be checked against the in-string mask. CLMUL quote pairing remains O(1) per block, but the effective field-boundary density drops dramatically (most structural chars are masked). Row prediction fails because embedded newlines make row lengths highly variable. Zero-copy fails because every field needs unescape processing. Throughput degenerates toward scalar parser speed.
anomaly_results.insight: Need a dedicated 'fully-quoted' fast path that skips delimiter scanning and focuses on quote-pair boundary detection. The worst case for SIMD CSV is still bounded by CLMUL throughput, not by branches.

anomaly_results.constraint: What if the file is 100% ASCII digits with comma separation (no quotes)?
anomaly_results.analysis: This is the ideal case. No quotes means CLMUL is a no-op (all zeros). Structural detection runs at maximum throughput. Row prediction is highly accurate (fixed-width rows). Columnar materialization is simple. Phase 2 is dominated by numeric parsing. Overall throughput should be limited only by memory bandwidth or numeric conversion speed.
anomaly_results.insight: For this case, the bottleneck shifts entirely to Phase 2 (number parsing). Consider fusing field detection with inline numeric conversion for pure-numeric files.

anomaly_results.constraint: What if we must parse from a network stream (no seek, no mmap)?
anomaly_results.analysis: Cannot mmap. Must buffer input in application memory. The two-phase architecture still works — Phase 1 operates on each buffered chunk, producing a structural index that Phase 2 processes before the buffer is reused. However, we lose the zero-copy benefit since we can't keep the input buffer around. The speculative row prediction becomes more valuable here because it allows pre-allocating output buffers before the full chunk is scanned.
anomaly_results.insight: A streaming mode that processes 1MB chunks through the full pipeline is essential. The structural index must be compact enough to fit in L2 cache alongside the input chunk.

anomaly_results.constraint: What if we inject a 100GB file on a machine with only 2GB RAM?
anomaly_results.analysis: mmap will page-fault through the file. Phase 1 structural index for 100GB could be multiple GB itself (one offset per field). Must process in streaming windows. Row prediction becomes critical for managing memory pressure. Column buffers must be flushed periodically.
anomaly_results.insight: Need a streaming/windowed mode with bounded memory. Emit Arrow RecordBatches at regular intervals (e.g., every 64K rows), flushing to downstream consumers. The structural index must be bounded-size, covering only the current window.
